Element.attribute: Conduct designed solution change impact analysis

Depending on how the program is set-up, the practitioner may need to execute the analysis twice: once during the high level design, and then again in the detailed design. Given the importance of this activity, it is recommended the analysis be executed during both high level and detailed designs, on large scale, multi-release, multi-year and multi-geographic transformations.

Executing the analysis is an essential activity, since it enables the practitioner to determine the level of impact against people, processes and systems that any proposed change will have on the organization. The analysis will also help determine the actions needed to both mitigate the degree of change and prepare the business to receive the change.

Detailed level Change Impact Analysis

Determine the criteria to execute the analysis. It is common to use people, processes and systems as criteria. Other dimensions can include: behavior and culture, structure, roles and capabilities, interaction and technology. The Change Impact Analysis tool should then be populated with the applicable criteria. Determine how to measure the level of impact (i.e., what constitutes a high, medium and low impact). The level of impact should be defined with the client and by taking the business into account, since each program is different. Determine whether the metrics to use should be quantitative, qualitative or both (e.g., 80% and above of ’X’ role will require new equipment to execute the role if the process change equals high impact).

Identify the subject matter resources (SMRs) who will be interviewed to determine the degree of change against people, processes and systems. Depending on the SMRs level of involvement with the program, carry out any additional engagement activities to secure SMR time and buy-in. Determine how to execute the Change Impact Analysis (e.g., should the analysis be executed through a workshop setting, one-on-one interviews, or both), and schedule interviews or workshops with the appropriate SMRs. Determine the detailed questions to ask SMRs during the scheduled interviews. Execute the high-level analysis and populate the Change Impact Analysis tool. Once the interviews and workshops are complete, identify the potential impact that the proposed solutions will have on: systems; people; team structures, reporting lines, potential employee numbers and location; role responsibilities and skills required; specific operations; organizational structures; and new and different behaviors and ways of working. Document findings from the high-level analysis in the action plan and establish the actions required to close the change gap. Engage other program workstreams to ensure the findings are shared and the change can be executed (e.g., training design and roll-out, procedures development). Share the high-level findings with the appropriate governance forum (e.g., BRIG).

When executing the detailed analysis, consider the criteria to use in determining the degree of change to drill- into the next level of detail (i.e. concentrating on teams, scenarios and roles). It is typical to use the Team, Scenario, and Roles Change Impact Analysis to fully understand the change impact:

1) Conduct the Team Change Impact Analysis:

  • Identify change impacts by capability (i.e., what are the skills and qualities needed to execute).
  • Analyze change impacts.
  • Develop an understanding of the future system landscape.
  • Develop an understanding of the current systems and determine system changes.
  • Map the change impacts to key teams within the organization structure, and develop an understanding of the structure and teams within the organization.
  • Draft the team impact analysis by identifying key process and system changes for each team.
  • Validate the team impacts with SMRs within the program and the business.

2) Conduct the Scenario Change Impact Analysis:

  • Map the activities in each scenario or process to the unique roles with key program representatives (e.g., capability workstreams, solution teams, technology partners).
  • Identify the change impacts for each scenario at the process or task level (e.g., technology, role and capabilities, interactions).
  • Summarize the change impacts for each scenario to feed into the interviews or workshops.
  • Validate the key change impacts for each scenario with SMRs.
  • Once the interviews or workshops have been conducted, consolidate the scenario change impacts for each unique role into a role-impact matrix.
  • Develop a record of process efficiencies and inefficiencies. This will show the areas in which efficiency improvements should be realized.
  • Validate roles for each step within the scenarios.
  • Analyze the scenario output to complete the step-level Change Impact Analysis for each scenario (i.e. look at each step in the scenario), including structure, behavior and culture impacts.
  • Conduct workshops with the relevant management stakeholders to validate the step-level change impact analysis.

3) Conduct the Roles Change Impact Analysis:

  • Develop a unique roles list for the Change Impact Analysis.
  • Analyze the roles list from human resources (HR).
  • Identify unique roles from a change impact perspective. Roles with the same purpose, similar duties and that require similar skillsets are not considered unique.
  • Validate the unique roles list with the internal and external program teams, department heads, and SMRs.
  • Develop the draft roles impact analysis.
  • Understand the key activities of unique roles and the systems used through discussions with SMRs within the program and the business.
  • Develop role impacts with the team leads in the business.
  • Consolidate the final impacts into each role based on scenario impacts, and validate with the program and business.
  • Document the findings from the detailed Change Impact Analysis and establish the actions required to close the change gap. Engage other program workstreams to ensure the findings are shared and the change can be executed (e.g., training design and roll-out, procedure development).
  • Share the findings with the appropriate governance forum (e.g., BRIG).
  • Once the Change Impact Analysis has been conducted, the insights learned will then be turned into tangible actions to enable the expected change impact on a role or function to be reduced. It is important to write a report with the key findings against the assessed impact areas, and develop an action plan of the activities to be conducted to minimize the change impact.
